newsitem.title: JORDAN: Jordan investors buoyed by new reforms.
newsitem.headline: Jordan investors buoyed by new reforms.

text.p: Jordan's move to enact into law two major reforms to overhaul the stock market and modernise company legislation will help its bourse lure foreign investors, investment managers said on Sunday.

A royal decree passed on Saturday enacting the new securities law also lifts the last legal hurdle to the passage of an overhauled companies law, which the government had put on hold after approving it three months ago.
The new company law cancels a 15 percent tax on companies raising their capital bases by shifting money from reserves.

The new securities law, the first major overhaul of the bourse since it was set up in 1978, permits dual listing of Jordanian firms on the Amman bourse and international exchanges, encourages Jordanian Global Depository Receipts, and allows the listing of mutual funds on the stock market for the first time.

It will also set up within two years an automated central depository settlement system and will restrict the duties of the bourse management to those of a regulator, leaving operations in the hands of the private sector.
The two pieces of reform are part of a wider package of economic reforms awaiting legislative action to improve the business climate.
"Yes of course there will be a noticeable increase in foreign buying," said Ziad Basha, securities manager at Jordan's British Bank of the Middle East.

News that the two laws had been approved injected fresh optimism into Amman's beleaguered stock exchange on Sunday. Shares rose across the board in busy trade and the official Amman Financial Market index climbed 0.71 percent.

Investment managers say earlier delays in passing the laws had hampered trade over the last two months in leading blue-chip shares, which had risen on expectations of bonus share issues. The firms promised shareholders they would boost their capital with transfers from reserves, including free share offers.
Analysts expect those promises to be fulfilled soon now that the laws have been approved.
"What we see is at least 30 companies which will issue bonus shares and create a supply of needed shares," said Basha.

Investment analysts say more supply of stock in firms that have currently reached a maximum foreign ownership ceiling will also address a serious shortage of so-called free float in the market, seen by emerging funds as a major hindrance to investment.

Three stocks alone -- Arab Bank, Islamic Bank and Arab Potash -- account for 52 percent of the market's capitalisation of 3.5 billion dinars ($4.9 billion). The first two have reached a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling and the third has only 0.08 percent free floating shares.

The companies law is also expected to improve the business climate by scrapping the state's issuing committee, which sets prices of new share issues, and waiving a 10 percent ownership ceiling for a single founder in initial public offerings.
"They have created the momentum right now and they now need to maintain it," Basha said.
He said the government should act quickly on recommendations to scrap the 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling hindering outside fund buying.

Wider foreign ownership and a set privatisation timetable would accelerate foreign inflows to Jordan's bourse, whose 1997 price/earnings ratio of 10.7 compares favourably with Egypt, Morocco and Lebanon, regional rivals for investment. - Amman Newsroom +9626 623 776
